article: The stomach is not an empty bag with acid in the bottom, where food plops in and dissolves. It's an expandible sac lined with acidic mucus. Gravity actually plays a very small part in digestion even here on Earth. Most of the action, including in the stomach, is a result of muscles pushing the food around, not gravity pulling it down. Check out [this animation] (URL0).,Human digestive system doesn't work only on gravity. When you swallow food, muscles in your throat and your intestines "push" it down to your stomach. While stomach is often pictured as balloon with acid on bottom, it doesn't just stand like that. Many muscles in stomach are contracted and everything inside is mushing around, mixing with acid. Also stomach doesn't have fixed size but it adjusts itself according to amount of food you ate. There is very little "empty space.,'Followup question; is acid reflux more prevalent in people who are in weightless environments?','To add to Mikepants's explanation, the stomach has 3 layers of muscle lining it. Each layer of muscle is laid down with fibers running in different directions. Functionally, this means the stomach can make complex "wringing" motions to aid in the churning of food as well as aid in pushing it into the small intestine. Gravity plays little role in waste excretion. Once food leaves the stomach, rhythmic, wave-like contractions push what used to be food through the small then large intestines. These wave-like contractions are referred to as peristalsis. Peristaltic contractions are also used in getting urine from the kidneys to the bladder, so gravity is not necessary for urinating in space either.','OP, have you ever drank water upside down to get rid of hiccups?

article: Humans are incredibly complex. Two people who grew up with an alcoholic dad, 1 could end up a teatotaler and one an alcoholic, and both claim that it was because of their dad that they made that choice. Science generally throves on the idea that anyone could recreate an experiment and get the same results. The problem is that it is impossible in the social sciences to completwly recreate an experiment. It is different subjects, or a different time of day, or different weather that say that impacted moods, or different things in the news, or different breakfast the subjects ate that morning. Now, this doesn't mean it is worthless. It just means that all it can do is speak on trends, in "more likely," in x influences y, in probabilities. These findings can be super valuable and can be as influential to society, but especially to a scientific mind searching for certainty and replicability, it can seem a bit wishy washy. Also the fields suffer from a publication bias (as many do, but it seems harsher in social sciences). Basically people don't want to publish articles about how nothing happened. So say 20 psychologists are testing if popcorn makes you like a movie more. At each school they have a group with popcorn and a group without popcorn rate a movie. At 19 schools they find.... nope, doesn't look like it. At 1 school they find the popcorn average is a bit higher. The last school gets published, the first 19 get ignored (not maliciously.... just because "nothing happened" doesn't seem interesting). Now newspaper articles across the country say "psychologist show eating popcorn makes you like movies more!" When really say showed "if you do enough experiments, one is bound to be an outlier and show something." This is the "replicability issue" facing a lot of classic studies. So, in summary.... it isn't a worthless field. But it cannot provide the same level of precise if-this-then-that that other sciences can because they are studying a subject (people) that are too complex to completely model currently.', "Because the social sciences aren't particularly rigorous. 1. Observational vs. empirical science. In an empirical science, you can create experiments where you isolate the elements of concern and test them without interference from other factors. In an observational science, you're simply looking at the results of processes over which you have no control. As a result, observational sciences aren't very rigorous - you don't have a very clear notion of whether what you're seeing is due to a valid observation or simply reading too much into the'noise' of the data set. 2. Quantitative vs. qualitative science. Any time you're forced to describe a phenomenon strictly in words, that means you don't really understand the phenomenon well enough to precisely identify it. Shakespeare would describe love in words - a non-scientific definition. A neuroscientist would describe it in terms of brain chemistry - a scientific one. 3. Reproducibility. Science exists independent of the researcher. So whenever you have a scientific result, other researchers should be able to validate that result using the same principles as the original researcher. However, this is almost never the case with social sciences because the conditions of the original research are either impossible to duplicate or involve holistic elements that are poorly understood. When you see results that are not derived from isolated experimentation, do not provide reproducibility and are not expressed in terms of quantitative measures, you're not really talking about'science'. You're talking about a particular philosophy of one sort or another. That philosophy might well be convincing or help you understand a phenomenon better, but it doesn't have the degree of confidence that we place in science.

article: a lock out is the opposite of a strike, the owners are not letting the employees work until a new contract is negotiated. The contract between players and owners expired this year. Players and owners needed to make a new contract that would establish how they split up the money they earn (ProfitRevenue). Owners don't want to give up more than 47 of the money that the NBA as a whole earns. Players want 50. Players do not want a hard cap on salary, meaning that teams have a set maximum for total salary to all players on the roster. The owners want to reduce the minimum salary. Owners are also complaining about the economic conditions of small-market teams such as (Toronto, The Pacers, The Bucks) versus large market teams (Heat, Boston, Lakers). The major source of contention is splitting the Profit, the latest deal offered by owners was 49 of the money with a hard salary cap. Players did not like this deal and felt that the union, who is negotiating the deal on their behalf, was not doing a good enough job on their behalf, they want to leave the union (de-certify) and go to court for an anti-trust lawsuit. anti-trust being laws that are suppose to prevent monopolies, which the NBA has on professional basketball in the US.,Decertification is kind of sham to make it easier to sue the NBA. When the players join a union, they transfer some of their rights to the union. But since the union is a group, it can only sue for things that damages players as a group. So the union is basically saying "let's pretend we are not a union for a while." During that time, players can sue the NBA as individuals...and a couple hundred lawsuit has really tie up NBA lawyers. Then, after they get some sort of agreement, they form a wink wink nudge nudge "new" union, and act like it never happened.', "Basically the owners are claiming that the NBA doesn't make enough money and that most teams actually lose money. This claim may be true, but it's somewhat dubious as the NBA won't release all their financial data. The Collective Bargaining Agreement or CBA, which is the contract between the players and owners expired, so they need a new one. The owners want to keep a certain percentage of Basketball Related Income, or BRI, which covers everything from tickets to jerseys to the tv deal. They also want a hard salary cap set at a certain number. The players want to keep a higher percentage of BRI and they want a soft cap, which means teams are only allowed to go over a certain salary based on certain exemptions. It's really convoluted and complicated. The players decertifying means they break up their union so they can sue the NBA. It's basically just the process where they end private negotiations and go to the courts because they can't reach a compromise.," "A bit of background information: just like other jobs, playing in professional sports often includes a collective bargaining agreement, or an agreement between the managers and workers setting the rules for hiring people. In basketball, this includes things such as rules of trading players, contracts, how revenue is distributed, maximum and minimum player salaries, the rules for the NBA draft, salary caps for teams, exceptions to the salary cap, and so forth. The NBA's last CBA was signed in June, 2005 and ended June 30th, 2011. Much like normal contractsalary negotiations, they are are centered around what you would naturally assume they would be centered on. The NBA (the commissioner David Stern and the 30 NBA owners) wants less costs, while the player's association wants highersimilar salaries. The NBA wants a hard salary cap (which means that teams are not allowed to go over a certain total that they spend on player salaries) at a lower level (so they spend less money, which means they can make more) while the player's associations wants to keep a soft cap (which means that teams have more exceptions, so players can make more). The focus of the lockout is about the BRI, or basketball related income. This determines the revenue sharing between the league and the players. It's a bit complicated, but they total amount of salaries and benefits given to players through agreed upon contracts can't go over the amount that they agreed to through the CBA revenue sharing agreement. If, for instance, it's set to 50 and the salaries and benefits of the players are worth a total of 51 million while the league makes 100 million, the 1 million for the players that would go over the set 50 would be given back to the league instead (there is a process where they hold a certain amount from paychecks, usually 8-10, and then they check the BRI and payments at the end of the season). As for decertifying, it means that the players no longer accept that the union is their legitimate representative to the owners. The threat of decertifying would mean that in the event of a lockout, players could bring individual or class-actions lawsuits against the league for antitrust violation, that is, the NBA committed unfair business practices to create a monopoly. Just as a side note, but this has been done before in the Big 4 Sports, most recently in March of this year when the NFL player's association briefly decertified allowing Drew Brees, Tom Brady, and Peyton Manning to bring forward a class-action lawsuit (Brady, et al. v. National Football League, et al.). Edit: For those interested, USA Today obtained a copy of the last proposal (WARNING: PDF) put forward by the league. The players rejected it today. article: They aren't powers of 360. They are multiples of 360. A power of 360 would be represented as 360720," "It makes scaling between them simpler. For some time, for the sake of backwards-compatibility, it's best to scale old content up rather than re-master it. Think of a tiny picture with 2x2 pixels. And two new displays with 3x3 pixels and 4x4 pixels. To scale the image up to the 4x4 display is simple enough. Just repeat each pixel twice. But the 3x3 will be a pain. If you repeat the first pixel, but not the second since you can't, the image will stay sharp but distort. If you count the average from neighboring pixels and fill the extra pixels with that, the image won't distort but won't be sharp either. Or you can keep the 2x2 image and fill the rest with black bars. A 5x5 display would similarly sucks but 6x6 would be sweet again. I'm only using small numbers to make up a worst-case scenario. It all kind of blends in the mass when the resolutions are in the thousands. But it's still noticeable. To see what I mean in real-life, for a distorted image, try setting a 4:3 resolution in your 16:9 monitor. Everything will stretch wider. And for blurry image, try setting a resolution that's close to your display's native resolution but not exactly it. For example 1050p for 1080p display. Depending on how your monitor handles things, it may add the black bars or do the averaging thing. These you are more likely to find in-OS. On third-party applications that allow custom resolutions, it's possible to find even better (or worse) examples. So to scale up a 720p image to 1080p they have the option of repeating every other pixel. It's not optimal, but keeps the image similar enough. Same goes for 1080p to 1440p. from 1080p to 4k it's again repeating every pixel. From 720p to 1440p it's repeating every pixels. And of course, if the content is specially made for 1440p or 4k, it'll be pristine on those displays and to scale down to 1080p or 720p, they leave out pixels.,Modern Computer resolutions inherited their display sizes from a legacy of punch cards and the number of scan lines of cathode ray tubes. You see the original graphics resolution for PCs was VGA with 640x480 and most of the ones that came later like like SVGA (800x600) were based upon that. The VGA inherited the resolution from text based resolution where you did not display graphics but rather charters in for example an 80 by 25 or 80 by 60 grid. If you have an 80x60 grid and use 8by8 pixels per character you arrive at the original VGA resolution. The 80s characters per line is something far older that modern computer displays. IBM standardized on punch cards with 80 columns in 1928. So the whole 80 characters was sort of inherited from those type of equipment (also 72 characters were often used with teletypes for practical reasons.) This sort of gave you the horizontal resolution increments we still use to day. The vertical ones from your question came thanks to the combination of wanting nice square characters that were 8x8 pixels in the beginning and the whole thing being compatible with American TV screens which were based on NTSC which had 480 scan-lines. Early home computers used TVs as their display. So that was the limit they could use. Originally TVs were not digital like today but analogue. They did not have any pixels just a ray of electrons that wandered back and forth and down from the bottom across as specially made glass surface making it glow. Horizontally they theoretically did not have any resolution at all, but vertically it was divided into rows upon rows that they ray moved along. The original design used in the US had more than 480 of these, but not all of them were visible and in the end 480 were only used of what remained to get a nice round number. We have long since moved away from all the thing these values originally came from, but the steps to go from where we started tow here we ended up were all small and all were taken in mind with the idea of staying compatible with what came before.','It has less to do with "360" and more to do with the aspect ratio. article: From what I can tell, both are somewhat psychosomatic responses, though one makes more "scientific" sense than the other. article: Every part of the US federal government (and the CIA is a part of that government) is subjected to 3 forms of oversight: 1: The Congress funds it. Congressional funding only lasts for 1 or 2 years at a time before the funding must be renewed. If Congress doesn't fund it, the agency ceases operations. {There are tinfoil hat conspiracies that the CIA has accumulated secret slush funds, ownership interests in business, and profits from illegal activities which allow it to operate outside of these restraints. Even if it were true (and I doubt) that the CIA has access to funds outside of Congressional supervision, such funds would be a tiny, tiny part of its operating budget and aren't being used to fund anything other than very small, very covert operations.} 2: The President directs it. All the various agencies and departments of the US government work at the direction of the President. Their leadership are all appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate and they serve at the President's discretion. The CIA was created in the mid 1940s when the War Department was reorganized after WWII. Originally the Director of the CIA was a cabinet-level official who reported directly to the President. Today there's a level of bureaucracy in the middle, the Director of National Intelligence (a post created after 911 as a result of the 911 Commission's recommendations) but the head of the CIA still serves at the pleasure of the President. 3: The court system oversees it. The CIA must follow US law and if it does not follow the law the people who broke the law can be and are prosecuted. In addition, in the 1970s a special court was set up, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) court which reviews matters related to intelligence operations within the United States or targeting US persons. All these layers and checks balances are one reason the thunderous bloviation from the Congress about these matters rarely translates into any action. It plays well to the general public but in reality the US intelligence services are very well monitored and extremely well overseen.," "The head of the CIA reports to the Director of National Intelligence, who in turn is under the command of the President. In practice the head of the CIA deals with the DNI, Congress, and the White House. The media probably doesn't mention them together very often because their actions are very secretive.

article: Well, I certainly applaud anyone wanting to do a hundred pushups, but take it from this old gym rat, I've spent my entire adult life in the gym, and a program like this one can do more harm than good. If you only train one part of your body (and that's all a single exercise like pushups is going to do for you), you're setting yourself up for injuries down the road. I've seen it a hundred times. It's like putting a powerful engine in a stock Toyota Tercel. What will you accomplish? You'll blow out the drive train, the clutch, the transmission, etc., because those factory parts aren't designed to handle the power of an engine much more powerful than the factory installed engine. Push-ups basically only train the chest muscles and to some extent, the triceps. What you really want to do is train your entire body, all the major muscle groups (chest, back, abdomen, legs, shoulders and arms) at the same time, over the course of a workout. And don't forget your cardiovascular work! I'm proud of you guys wanting to do this. Three cheers! Falling in love with exercise, eating right, etc., is one of the greatest things you can do for yourself. And you WILL fall in love with it if you can just force yourself to stick with it a year or two and experience the amazing progress you'll make. But do it right, okay? My advice, find a good gym, with qualified trainers who will design your programs for you (especially in the beginning, until you get the hang of it yourself) and guide you in your quest for physical fitness. Thirty to 45 minutes a day, three days a week, is all you'll ever need to do (I refuse to believe anyone is so busy that he or she cannot make time for that, especially considering how important it is). And don't worry about being embarrassed or not being in shape the first time you walk into the gym. You have to start somewhere and almost every one of us were there ourselves at one time. article: Duverger's law. Basically because we have a system where the winner takes all (so the president or congressman being elected represents 51 of the population at minimum) we naturally tend to split into the two party system. Imagine you have 10 people voting on what kind of pizza to order. Some are vegetarian and some are meat lovers. Whoever gets the most votes gets to order the pizza for everyone. Now, 4 people are vegetarians and will vote for the veggie lovers pizza, and 6 are meat-lovers. However, 3 of those 6 want pepperoni, and 3 want Canadian bacon. If you tally up the votes the vegetarians would win and get their way, even though more people wanted meat on their pizza, but because they split up over a smaller detail they lost all together. The same works for politics. If 45 are conservative and 55 are liberal, then you'd expect the democrats to win. However, if a socialist is also running and gets 15 of the liberal vote then the election turns out like this: 40 democrats, 45 republicans, and 15 socialists. So, even though more people are liberal and would vote democrat, because of the split in the Democratic Party the conservatives win the election. So if my first choice is socialist, and my second choice is democrat, if I vote socialist the democrats are all that more likely to lose to the republicans and the socialists never stood a chance anyway. So I essentially not only threw my vote away to a party that won't win, I took votes from my second favorite option and allowed the republicans to garner more votes overall,because of our voting structure. CGP Grey has a good and simple explanation of how this happens. People dislike the two party system now because it completely rigged - quite overtly at times - the political and electoral process. That's why there are so many complaints - they are complaints against the inability to influence the political system rather than the ability to have five parties instead of two. But it's not always a bad things - for example the much decried recent British election saved Britain from incompetence and rampant idiocy by restricting both the totally incompetent Greens and the disastrous UKIP - both essentially populist, protest parties with no capacity to rule or influence the political process - from parliament. It also introduces SNP to national politics - something which might be very refreshing (or not) considering that for long Labour was the choice of the home countries (other than England). So why do the people complain? Becuase they don't like Cameron - either on reasonable grounds or simply because they are ignorant and believe demagogues on the internet - and they want him gone, but they can't. The fact that the other choices are just as bad - if not overtly worse - don't matter because politics is not a fully rational field. On the other hand two party system is the most natural form of political representation - far more natural than those cumbersome multi-party, multi-mandate systems of Europe (all of which were historically invented to satisfy politicians - not voters! source: I'm European).All the alternative voting systems are extremely confusing while the two party system works on the age-old "you're gone, here's the other guy" which even the stupidest voter can comprehend. It also serves the same goal quite efficiently - contrary to what CGP Greys and other semi-knowledgeable internet pundits will tell you - unless it becomes restrictive in terms of access. In other words it isn't the "only two parties always win" (something which makes the power-hungry politicians from other parties raving mad) arrangement but the fact that the two parties suddenly get to control the electoral process and won't allow anyone who isn't in them to win. In other words the two party system wasn't a problem until it started getting in the way of voters voting for whomever they chose to vote for - instead of voting for the pre-approved candidates. Those two tings are very different and internet amateurs like CGP grey should stop pretending that they know anything, learn some non-English language and look into the politics of France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Scandinavia, Poland etc and realize that those multi-party, multi-mandate systems have the same problems. As a matter of fact right this very moment in Poland there is so much backlash against the current multi-party, multi-mandate political system that one of the leading opposition parties (a protest party) is one advocating British style electoral system!!!! How can it be? Unless both are missing the real issue... You can't solve the problem of politicians of two parties restricting voter influence by creating more parties. They will only take slightly more time to restrict voter influence again but they will do it anyway - always - because putting voters in their place is the first priority for every career politician no matter how many parties there are: fifty, ten, four, two.... or one. TL;DR - the number of parties is not the problem, the control parties have over the electoral process compared to the voters is.

article: Photo sensitive papers and films are made using a form of silver. The silver halides have a very low activation threshold, and the zap of a photon is enough to knock pieces off the halide, changing it's chemical structure. The film is made by using a substrate which is anything you use to hold the image. It could be plastic, paper, cellulose, etc. The base substrate is embedded with the silver halides and these impregnate the film or paper. It is then dried and packaged in light proof containers. The image is developed using a developer compound like D76, which is a powder dissolved into water to form a liquid developer. It darkens or tarnishes the exposed silver particles. The reaction will keep going until a chemical neutralizer called stopbath is used. Stopbath reacts with the developer and neutralizes it so it stops developing. Without it, an image would continue to get darker and darker over time as the developer continued to work long after it was in a darkroom. Finally the film or paper is run through a chemical called a fixer. It renders the rest of the silver halides inert and they will no longer react with light. At this point you can flip the lights on because you have a permanent photograph or negative, once you wash it off. A fun fact, the silver collected in the film and paper ends up saturating the fixer tray. It is possible to recover the silver from the liquid by chemically treating it and then refining. It doesn't amount to much but it's still pretty cool.

article: Console pick a resolution and stick with it. If the target is 720p, the game will render at 1280x720 and upscale to 1920x1080 or downscale to 852x480. Games that have been scaled look like crap; PC gamers demand that games render at the native resolution of their monitor. Any game that doesn't is (properly) derided as crap. If there is only one resolution to render at, the designers can make a huge number of assumptions that greatly simplify development. Every user of a console game uses the same controller. The people that don't use that controller use a controller that emulates the normal controller. On the other hand, PC gamers not only demand that games work with whatever bizarre keyboard or speed pad or keypad or joystick they own, but they demand that the game allows buttons to be remapped to suit their similarly bizarre purposes. Ask 100 different WoW players what buttons do what and you'll get 150 different responses. Every console has the same CPU, the same video card, the same amount of RAM, the same storage medium, and none of them have any processes running in the background. If a game encounters a slowdown in a certain situation, the game will always slow down there on every single console owned by every single user every single time. You can then optimize that section or cut detail in that section. On the other hand, some PCs are CPU limited, some PCs are GPU limited, some PCs are memory bandwidth limited, some PCs are memory quantity limited, some PCs have more or less disk space or disk speed, some PCs have resident programs (malware, malware scanners, a browser that was left open with a flash animation running, crappy OEM software like picture organizers that are always running, the hideous monstrosity that is HP's printer suite) that sop up any given resource, and you typically can't predict the slow parts. You'll need to expose every detail setting to the user to enable them to configure it, and then you'll need to know when the user is a fucking moron and override some of their settings if you need to. Video cards from ATI and nVidia behave much differently. There are differences between each generation of video cards, sometimes drastic ones. You need a few different rendering paths, and need to pick the right one depending on what hardware is available. Consoles do not have this problem. Other devices can have similar problems (sound cards might perform certain functions slowly or at the use of a lot of CPU) and in all cases you need to be more tolerant of whacky inputs. PC gamers are, to varying degrees, tolerant of bugs at launch, console gamers are not. article: I used to work as a baggage handler. When your bag is checked, it is put on a conveyor belt and sent down to the bag room where workers wait at a baggage carousel similar to the one the passengers use. A worker will be assigned to your flight and will be looking for bags tagged for your flight. Most bags will not be connecting to other flights and are all packed together in the hold. But connecting bags are loaded on to a separate cart and typically loaded last and kept slightly apart from the rest of the bags. The ramp workers at the connecting airport will know the exact number of connecting bags and will grab them first, load them onto a cart and whisk them directly to the connecting flight. When the aircraft is loaded, the bags are usually separated based on if they are cityterminating bags, priority terminating bags, transfer bags that stay with the airline, and transfer bags. In most cases, they are segregated into separate sections in the aircraft, or pits in the case of narrowbody, non container aircraft, or bag containers, or ULDs with wide body aircraft. With our software, we know what plane you bag was loaded onto, where it is in the aircraft or container, what sequence it was scanned into it and your routing. So when a plane arrives, we have a dedicated group of baggage handlers that will come and pick up your bags. They are given the assignment beforehand and know how many bags they are picking up, what type of bag, their destination and the departure time. On our mainline flights, there will be multiple runners that have specific tasks, some could be there just for the "hot" bags, bags that have a connection of less than an hour. These guys will take the bags and deliver each bag to the waiting aircraft. The "cold" runners will take all the bags that have connection times of an hour or more and drop them all off to a cold input belt that goes to the baggage sorter, where they will be brought up later. An example of nature of how specific enzymes can be can be seen in glucose polymers. Glucose polymers in alpha bond configurations are what most organisms digest for easy carbohydrate energy. article: Also Known as Pack Hardening, Blister Steel, Shear Steel From what I understand from reading old texts, traditionally, case hardening was a technique were a blacksmith would infuse a piece of iron or steel with carbon to create a hard outer layer while keeping the inside softer and more malleable. This was done by heating the metal in a carbon-rich environment, usually with charcoal or bone charcoal, and then quenching it in water or oil to harden the outer layer. This process was often used to make tools or weapons that needed to be tough and durable on the outside, but still somewhat flexible on the inside. Blister steel and shear steel were types of steel produced by a similar process, but with higher carbon content. Blister steel was made by heating wrought iron in a sealed container with a carbon source, which caused the iron to absorb carbon and form bubbles of carbon monoxide gas. The resulting steel was then forged and cut into bars or sheets. Shear steel was made by heating wrought iron and pieces of blister steel together in a crucible or furnace, which created a homogenous blend of steel with a high carbon content. This steel was then forged and cut into blades for knives or swords, which were known for their sharpness and durability. Overall, case hardening and related techniques were important ways that blacksmiths could manipulate the properties of iron and steel to create tools and weapons with specific characteristics. While modern methods of steel production and heat treatment have largely replaced these traditional techniques, they still have a place in the history of metallurgy and the development of technology.

article: Black and White film has one emulsion, color film has three emulsions (RGB). According to [Wikipedia] (URL0): Photographic emulsion is a fine suspension of insoluble light-sensitive crystals in a colloid sol, usually consisting of gelatin. The light-sensitive component is one or a mixture of silver halides: silver bromide, chloride and iodide. The gelatin is used as a permeable binder, allowing processing agents (e.g., developer, fixer, toners, etc.) in aqueous solution to enter the colloid without dislodging the crystals. Other polymer macromolecules are often blended,[citation needed] but gelatin has not been entirely replaced. The light-exposed crystals are reduced by the developer to black metallic silver particles that form the image. Colour films and papers have multiple layers of emulsion, made sensitive to different parts of the visible spectrum by different colour sensitizers, and incorporating different dye couplers which produce superimposed yellow, magenta and cyan dye images during development. Panchromatic black-and-white film also includes colour sensitizers, but as part of a single emulsion layer. Most modern emulsions are "washed" to remove some of the reaction byproducts (potassium nitrate and excess salts). The "washing" or desalting step can be performed by ultrafiltration, dialysis, coagulation (using acylated gelatin), or a classic noodle washing method. Emulsion making also incorporates steps to increase sensitivity by using chemical sensitizing agents and sensitizing dyes. The number of emulsions affects the quality and the volume of byproducts that had to be removed.

article: All aeroplanes are steered with control surfaces. "Ailerons" on the outer edges of the wings move up and down to cause the aeroplane to roll left and right. "Elevators" on the horizontal tailplane move up and down to cause the nose of the aircraft to point up or down. And the "rudder" on the vertical tailplane moves left and right, to cause the nose of the aircraft to point left or right. In a simple aircraft, these control surfaces are moved by being directly connected to the pilots' controls by cables and pulleys. In most airliners, the controls are too heavy to be moved by cables. Instead, the pilots' controls directly command a hydraulic system to move the control surfaces. If the pilot pulls back on the controls, the hydraulics immediately cause the elevators to move, so the aircraft's nose points up. In fly-by-wire systems, the controls do not directly affect the hydraulics. Instead, the position of the controls is fed to a computer. The computer processes this information, possibly combining it with other information. It is then the computer which instructs the hydraulics to move the flying surfaces. There are lots of advantages of this. In Airbus aircraft, it allows the computer to be put into different modes for different phases of flight, adjusting how the controls respond to pilot inputs. It allows the computer to override the pilot in certain circumstances. It also allows the computer to process the input from the two pilots separately (although it's quite debatable whether this is an advantage or a disadvantage). In the Eurofighter Typhoon, fly-by-wire is essential. The aircraft design is inherently unstable. This allows it to outmanoeuvre pretty much any other aircraft - but it means that the control inputs which have to be made just to keep it flying in a straight line are too difficult for a human pilot to be able to do. The pilot instructs the computer, using normal flying controls, and the computer works out what needs to be done to not only comply with the pilot's requests, but also to overcome the instability of the aircraft, and it combines these two things together and moves the control surfaces accordingly.

article: That is called bootstrap problem. How can you program something when no software exists that lets you program things. And how can a computer read what to do, if it has no instructions to begin with? One possible solution to the bootstrap problem is to start with a set of very basic instructions written in machine language (the language that computers speak), and use those instructions to build more complex instructions and programs. This process is also known as bootstrapping or self-hosting. For example, a programmer could start with the most basic machine instructions to add, subtract, and compare numbers, and then use those instructions to create more complex operations like conditional statements, loops, and functions. Over time, more complex programs and programming languages can be built upon this foundation. Another solution is to use a pre-existing programming language or tool to create the initial instructions or software needed to bootstrap a new system. This approach is common in the development of operating systems, where code is initially written in a higher-level language like C, and then compiled into machine code that can be run on a computer. Overall, there are several ways to approach the bootstrap problem, and the solution will typically depend on the specific goals and constraints of the project.

article: Biologist here. Here's an attempt: Your muscles consume energy. A lot of it. They use this energy in the form of a molecule called ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate), commonly called the "energy currency" of cells. Cells use this molecule by essentially harvesting the energy that is released when a single phosphate is broken off. The ATP that once was "triphosphate" becomes "diphosphate" (ADP) and your cells take up the energy to use for whatever they need. ADP is not very useful as most of the energy comes from that third bond, and just two phosphates don't really have as much energy, so your body needs some way to replenish that ADP back into ATP to use again. This is done through a fairly complex mechanism called "cellular respiration" where your cells use other sources of energy (food) to convert ADP back into ATP. So how does creatine fit into this? Well I mentioned how your muscles consume energy and there's only so many places you can get that energy. You have stores of ATP ready to be used in a moment's notice in your muscles, but depending on how quickly you use it up your body will need to replenish that ATP to keep going. You could get it from breaking down food and fat and using cellular respiration, right? Sure, but that takes SO long and we don't have time for that when we need to get that next set of reps in. So what creatine does is whenever your body is resting and you have excess ATP just sitting around, creatine will actually take up a phosphate and just hold onto it. When you start doing an intense workout all of a sudden like lifting something heavy, your skeletal muscles quickly deplete ATP into ADP and "creatine phosphate," being the cool dude he is, will come and donate his phopshate to that ADP, becoming ATP and able to do work again. The thing is, the creatine is only useful for about the first 2-10 seconds of intense workout. Effectively that means that it may help you get that 11th or 12th rep in, but once it's depleted and you're still exercising, it won't really serve a purpose until you take a break and allow your body to replenish both ATP and creatine phosphate. The other thing is your body can only have so much creatine because of this thing called "homeostasis." Having excess creatine from supplements causes your body to in turn produce less creatine. The swelling of muscles from creatine supplements comesf rom water wanting to flow into your muscle cells to counterbalance the change in concentration. This isn't very long lasting nor does it really affect much aside from making you look "swoll.

article: Milk is an emulsion of fatty globules suspended in water. We can ignore the fat for now, just note that it helps keep the dye from mixing in too fast. What we're really interested in is the water. Water is rather interesting for a molecule. It has a negatively charged end (the oxygen) and a positively charged end (the hydrogen), effectively making each water molecule act something like a bar magnet. When you put a bunch of water molecules together, they bunch up really tightly, giving water a lot of interesting characteristics. The key characteristic is a high surface tension. The surface of the water clings to itself very tightly, forming a sticky film. We're too big to feel it ourselves, but this is why [water strider bugs] (URL0) don't sink into the water. Soap is also interesting. It is usually a set of molecules with a hydrophilic (water-loving) head and a hydrophobic (water-fearing) tail. That's what gives it its cleaning power (dirt sticks to one end, water to the other, and everything gets washed away). Here, however, the soap gets in the way of the self-attraction of the water. With the surface tension broken, the rest of the water without soap contracts, bringing anything it's carrying (like dye) along with it. tl;dr: soap pops the film on the surface, the remains of which yank the dye to the side.

article: Two main processes were highlighted in the Microbiology book I have (Bauman, 2006). The first one consists of four basic steps, and the goal is to remove toxins and microorganisms which cause disease. One of the big steps in removing aerobic microorganisms is removing their oxygen source, which prevents them from breaking down nutrients. 1. Primary treatment - Wastewater is pumped into large tanks where it's allowed to settle. Lightweight solids, grease, and floating particles are skimmed off the top, and heavier materials settle on the bottom into sludge. A flocculating agent, alum, is added, which basically makes particles clump together and sink to the bottom of the tank to join the sludge. The sludge is then removed, and the water moves on to further treatment. 2. Secondary treatment - Basically, the water is aerated to facilitate the growth of microbes which will remove dissolved organic materials by metabolizing them into carbon dioxide or water. In the activated sludge system, the water is basically pumped into a sludgy mixture, where the microbes in the sludge start digesting what's left in the water. The water is then moved to an oxygen-free environment, and the sludge does its magic, removing oxygen, "starving" the remaining microbes. Smaller communities sometimes pass it through a sand filter in this step, but it's less effective. 3. Chemical treatment. The water is treated somehow, usually with chlorine, sometimes with UV or ozone. It's then either released into rivers or the ocean, or used to irrigate crops and highway vegetation. 4. Sludge treatment. More microbes are used to break down the sludge into carbon dioxide and other organic materials. The second system is artificial wetlands, which are pretty neat but require a much larger area. Essentially, the water is passed through a series of artificially-constructed ponds where the natural microbiota gradually break down the sediments and wastes. It's then treated (sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection via UV, chlorine, or ozone) and released back into the water supply. Hope this helps!','1. Water is collected in a single big deposit, like an artificial lake, or a tank. 2. Screening: This is when they remove large waste, mainly plastic and other things that don't dissolve in water, including bags, cotton, rags.... etc. This is pretty much like putting water through a sieve. 3. Primary Treatment: This is when they remove solid matter, in other words, poop. We're not worried about making the water drinkable yet, we just want to get the bulk of the waste out. This is done by putting the water into large tanks and literally letting it sit until all the solid sinks to the bottom. 4. Secondary treatment: The water now doesn't have any visible bits of solid, but it's still very filthy. This step is to remove smaller things out of the water, including insects and eggs. The water is put into active lanes and we pump air through the water (Bubbling) to encourage "good bacteria" growth. This bacteria will essentially killreduce 'bad bacteria'. 5. Tertiary treatment: The good bacteria has done it's job and now it needs to go as well. The water is placed back into another tank where it's allowed to settle. The bacteria sinks to the bottom and is removed like sludge from the bottom of the tank. 6. Sludge treatment: The process creates a large amount of waste (Mainly poop and bacteria) which is normally sludgy. The sludge is normally shipped off and either incinerated, or in some placed it gets pumped to gas recycling stations because it can generate a large amount of methane to be used as fuel.

article: We know that numbers whose decimal representation terminate have certain properties. Specifically, if N terminates, there must be two integers, X and Y, such that X Y N. So if a number has a terminating decimal representation, it can be written as a fraction ab, where a and b are integers and b has only 2 andor 5 as prime factors (because those are the only prime factors of 10, the base of our decimal system). Conversely, if a fraction can be expressed as ab, where b has only 2 andor 5 as prime factors, then its decimal representation will terminate (i.e., it will end in a finite number of digits). For example, the fraction 725 can be written as a terminating decimal: 0.28. In this case, 25 has only 2 andor 5 as prime factors (25 52), so 725 can be expressed as a terminating decimal. On the other hand, the fraction 13 cannot be expressed as a terminating decimal, because its denominator (3) has a prime factor other than 2 andor 5. Its decimal representation is 0.333333..., which goes on forever. Hope this helps!

article: When you clap, you send out sound waves. When two sound waves meet each other, they'interfere'. Imagine waves on water when you drop a stone into it. Peaks and troughs of the waves can either add up or cancel each other out, depending on their relative positions. Sound wave interference can be constructive or destructive. When two waves are in phase (their peaks and troughs line up), they will enhance each other and create a louder sound. This is called constructive interference. On the other hand, when two waves are out of phase (their peaks and troughs are opposite), they will cancel each other out and create silence. This is called destructive interference. Understanding sound wave interference is important in many fields, including music, acoustics, and telecommunications. It can also be useful in noise reduction and noise cancellation technologies.

However this time around the virus can only insert the DNA it was given earlier into the cells. article: MD5 is not "encryption" so to speak. To figure out how MD5 works, imagine you have a collection of numbers. Let's say: 1, 2, 3, 5, and 10. MD5 can create a "hash" of data, but let's create a much simpler hash algorithm for our data. The simplest way to do this is to add up our numbers: 1 2 3 5 10 21. This is deterministic. No matter how many times we add those numbers we'll always get the same answer. But there's a problem: we can't go back to the original data, because although our numbers add up to 21, so do a lot of other numbers. If we hashed some other numbers, like 10 and 11, we would also get 21 just the same. This is called a "collision." All hashing algorithms have collisions. The tricky part of designing a secure hash algorithm is to allow for possible collisions, but to minimize their existence as much as possible. To be unique, but not too unique. As long as a collision is possible, it is impossible to figure out what the original data was. This is why hashes are called one-way encryption. You cannot go back. A more ELI5 explanation: Imagine a peach and a nectarine. We take both the peach and nectarine and squish them in a very specific way. Now we can't really tell which one was a peach or nectarine (this is called a "collision, but we do know that whenever we squish a peachnectarine in this way, we'll always get the same kind of mess every single time. This is a way to verify that the original object was indeed a peach, but we can't tell exactly what kind of peach it was, and we can't tell its original shapeskincolor either. This is how MD5 and every other hashing algorithm works. It takes data and mangles it deterministically to the point where it's unrecognizable and impossible to figure out what the original data was. The problem with MD5 is that there are too many collisions: it's too easy to get the same kind of mess from different pieces of fruit.

There is a fairly new speciality in pharmacy (yes, there are pharmacists who specialize) called pharmacogenomics which studies these differences with the hope of better matching patients to drugs. (Blood pressure meds can have wildly different effects from patient to patient. That's why there are still so many different ones on the market.) Someday, we'll be able to use a person's genome to help physicians prescribe the proper drug rather than use the hit-and-miss method used now. Also, drugs can be designed for certain genotypes. (People with a certain gene or set of genes.) Resistance to certain drugs or unexpected effects from certain drugs are usually inherited. But even within a certain family, people maybe affected differently by the same drug at the same concentration. Also, people can become more tolerant to a drug if they are exposed to it a lot over time. This involves the liver and kidneys, which are the two major ways a drug is removed from the blood and therefore from the body. So, yes, people have different brain chemistry but some of the answers on here make it sound as though we're all wildly different in brain chemistry and that's just not true. There are subtle differences and some of them are physical rather than chemical. A drug must cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) to get into the nervous system. This barrier is a defense and the more "oily" a drug is, the easier it is for it to cross. (nonpolar vs. polar) A small difference in the effectiveness of the BBB can make a big difference in how much of a certain drug gets through. Also, the permeability of different parts of the brain to certain drugs can make a difference in which parts of the brain are most affected by a drug. Is it the reticular formation, which plays a big role in wakefulness? Is it the hippocampus, which is the major brain structure dealing with memory? Etc. And everyone is also right in that all of these things can change as we age. It seems nothing in the body undergoes more changes from birth to elderly death than the central nervous system. article: First, a bit of context. The United Nations, when founded, was divided into different organs, each with different responsibilities and obligations. When discussing the UN, most people tend to think of the General Assembly and the Security Council. The GA is the branch of the UN that includes all member states, with each having a single vote. In this chamber, all countries discuss topics of importance on a global scale or anything that is brought to its attention. The SC is the organ of the UN that deals, exclusively (with some exceptions), with matters of international peace and, as its name suggests, security. It is comprised of 15 members, 5 of who have a permanent seat as well as as the power to veto resolutions. These countries are: the United States, the People's Republic of China, Russia, France, and the United Kingdom. All other ten members have a vote but no veto power, and their positions are cycled through every 2 years or so. Now, please note the following. The United Nations Security Council will only use collective military action as its last resort. It will first analyze the situation, send envoys, investigate the assertion, and issue ceasefires or send peacekeeping forces to help ease tensions. If the conflict escalates then the SC will begin to use economic sanctions or blockades to end the violence. Military action is a last resort because the whole point of the UN is to solve conflicts between nations through diplomacy; war is the last option. So, using the Iraq War as a case-study, the United States, with the support of the United Kingdom, claimed that Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMDs) were, currently, under Iraq's possession and these provided an instant threat to the area and the globe. More context: These accusations, at the time, were considered extremely serious. The UN sanctions the proliferation of WMDs with severity, so it took the claims of the US and the UK with great care. As a consequence, the UNSC unanimously passed a resolution, 1441, which demanded Iraq let UN Weapon Inspectors in the country to verify the assertion that it had WMDs. This is where things get tricky. The inspectors, part of a branch of the UN known as UNMOVIC and the IAEA (Atomic Energy Agency), found no evidence of WMD production, with some exceptions. There were chemical rockets found and some long-range missiles were in direct violation to UN Disarmament Treaties. As such, these were destroyed under the supervision of UN Inspectors. However, these weapons, as well as other armament-related activity, contradictory evidence, and no assurance that chemical stockpiles had actually been destroyed, led the UN inspectors to determine Iraq, whilst following most of the provisions of Resolution 1441, had not cooperated "immediately" in some areas, one of the key points of the agreement. This final point, the lack of "immediacy," was what suggested to the United States that Iraq violated Resolution 1441. It demanded the UN get together to pass another, harsher resolution upon Iraq. As you now know, the only other option left was military intervention. However, by this point, other members of the SC, with the exception of the UK, demonstrated that they would veto ANY resolution that would lead to such an action. With no unanimous support within the permanent member block of the SC, the UN was virtually rendered incapable of doing anything else about Iraq. Nevertheless, all countries in the UN are sovereign, thus the US and the UK invaded Iraq without its approval on the matter, using the WMDs as its primary justification. TL;DR: The UNSC deals with matters of international security. It has a due process by which it can, as its last resort, suggest joint military intervention. The Iraq War, within the UN, was never approved of because it determined there was no evidence that WMDs were under the possession of Iraq.','URL0 France - On 20 January 2003, Foreign Minister Dominique de Villepin said, "We think that military intervention would be the worst possible solution" Russia - On the same day, Russian Foreign Minister Igor Ivanov said that "Russia deems that there is no evidence that would justify a war in Iraq." article: Firstly, downforce has far more to do with cornering than it does acceleration. Only in extremely high-powered vehicles is there the potential for the drive wheels to break traction at the kind of speeds where downforce-generating aero aids are effective. It's far more common for these'spoilers' to be employed to keep the vehicle stable during high speed cornering. For this reason, the comment about them being useless on front-wheel-drive vehicles is entirely incorrect. Aerodynamic aids can (and most definitely are) built into the front of vehicles to create downforce over the front wheels. Without these downforce-generating structures, the general shape of a vehicle (flat on the bottom, curved over the top) can often imitate the function of a plane's wing - the lower air pressure over the top of the vehicle causes lift to be generated at high speeds, leading to instability. Generally this is insignificant on normal road-going passenger vehicles, but high performance sports car, supercars, and race cars are often capable of speeds where it can be an issue. A related factor is weight. Normal passenger vehicles are usually noticably heavier than their sportsrace counterparts. The extra weight provides a downward force on the tyres, improving the lateral grip during cornering. As a result, no (or minimal) aero aids are needed. However, in race cars weight is considered (for the most part) undesirable as it has negative effects on acceleration and handling. So, how do you get the benefit of weight (the downward push on the tyres that increases grip) without the extra mass that creates inertia and resists changes of direction? You use air to push down on the car. The force is applied, but you aren't penalised by carrying extra mass. There's a downside to this though - more aerodynamic downforce creates more drag. Cornering improves, but top speed suffers. Booooo! Huge amounts of time and money are spent on tuning the aerodynamic properties of high performance vehicles to balance the application of downforce to improve cornering, and the minimisation of drag to maximise top speed and acceleration.," "The harder the tires are pressed down, the less they'll slide or spin, so a spoiler on a real race car helps the car stay stuck to the road. One-time-pad involves generating a random key that is the same length as the plaintext (the message you want to encrypt), and adding each corresponding character in the key to the plaintext. The resulting ciphertext (the encrypted message) cannot be decrypted without the key, which must be kept secret from anyone who is not authorized to see the message. One-time-pad is often considered unbreakable, as long as the key is truly random, used only once, and kept completely secret.

If you permanently delete a file, the implication (to an IT expert) is that you've gone out of your way to make sure that data is not there any more. As in, you used a program that actually goes to where that file's data was and overwrites it quite a few times using random data, as well as marking it as no longer there.','On a normal hard drive, files are not actually deleted when you "delete it permanently." What happens is that area of the hard drive where the file resided is no longer listed as the file in the file system, meaning that another file can overwrite that area. But before this, the data is still there and can be recovered using software. On all modern SSDs on a modern OS, things are handled differently. Due to how flash storage functions, simply marking the area of a deleted file as free space and leaving the data there degrades write speed as the drive fills with and writes over deleted data. So modern OSes have what's called a TRIM command. As soon as a file is deleted on an SSD, that space is immediately overwritten with zeroes.', "They don't actually get moved anywhere else or deleted, they are just no longer marked as anything, so when you go to save something else later on it can be saved over the top of what you have deleted, that's why sometimes it's possible to rescue deleted files, because nothing has replaced them yet

article: Not only do different age groups need different amounts of sleep, but sleep needs are also individual. Just like any other characteristics you are born with, the amount of sleep you need to function best may be different for you than for someone who is of the same age and gender. While you may be at your absolute best sleeping seven hours a night, someone else may clearly need nine hours to have a happy, productive life. In fact, a 2005 study confirmed the fact that sleep needs vary across populations, and the study calls for further research to identify traits within genes that may provide a "map" to explain how sleep needs differ among individuals. Another reason there is "no magic number" for your sleep results from two different factors that researchers are learning about: a person's basal sleep need - the amount of sleep our bodies need on a regular basis for optimal performance - and sleep debt , the accumulated sleep that is lost to poor sleep habits, sickness, awakenings due to environmental factors or other causes. Two studies suggest that healthy adults have a basal sleep need of seven to eight hours every night, but where things get complicated is the interaction between the basal need and sleep debt. For instance, you might meet your basal sleep need on any single night or a few nights in a row, but still have an unresolved sleep debt that may make you feel more sleepy and less alert at times, particularly in conjunction with circadian dips , those times in the 24-hour cycle when we are biologically programmed to be more sleepy and less alert, such as overnight hours and mid-afternoon. article: Chess was "westernized" a bit, the queen piece was originally called an advisor for the king who often wielded the true power while the king held a more ceremonial position. Yes, that's correct. The game of chess originated in the Indian subcontinent and was called chaturanga. In this game, the piece we now call the queen was known as the counselor or advisor, and it could only move one square diagonally. Later, when the game spread to Persia, the counselor was replaced by the firzan, a more powerful piece that could move diagonally any number of squares. When chess made its way to Europe in the Middle Ages, the firzan became the queen, and its movement was expanded to include horizontal and vertical movement as well. Thus, the game became more dynamic and exciting to play.

article: Heartburn is the colloquial term for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Your stomach has two "valves" at either end. At the top is the lower esophageal sphincter, this is the border between your esophagus (tube food goes down when you swallow) and stomach. Your stomach is lined with special cells that secrete mucous to protect themselves from acid. Heartburn occurs when stomach acid makes its way past this sphincter and begins to irritate the cells of the esophagus that do not have the special protective mucous layer. There are several different causes of heartburn, from bacterial infection (h. pylori) to insufficiency in the sphincter itself. To help alleviate the symptoms you can use over the counter antacids such as alka-seltzer and try to avoid laying down for several hours after eating (or if you must lay down, try to lay on your left side so gravity helps keep the acid in your stomach. For more severe and recurrent heartburn you should see a doctor and they'll give you medication to help prevent too much acid production (Histamine-2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors) or fight an h. pylori infection. GERD can be a very serious problem and I highly recommend you see a doctor if it is a regular problem for you. Continually irritating your esophagus with acid can cause strictures or a condition called Barrett's Esophagus which can lead to esophageal cancer.', "It's usually an excess of acid in your stomach. Or, your stomach is too full, and it's contractions push some of the digestive juices up into your esophagus. Or, if you're on your backright side, and the valve the closes your stomach off from the esophagus doesn't seal, some of your stomach acids can flow into your esophagus. I'm not going to claim this is the best explanation, but as a general idea it's good enough

article: A lot of nausea is produced by a disconnect between what your body is feeling and your eyes are seeing (which the body may interpret as having been poisoned). When reading in a car for instance, your body is feeling bumps but your eyes see a stable frame. Watching the road connects and anticipates the way your body is experiencing the road. Being the driver and having control of the movement can be even better 3d movies can be the opposite for some people. Your brain thinks you should be moving, but your body is stationary. Looking of the screen at an exit sign or a seat back recalibrates you.', "When the ground in front of you is heading toward you rapidly, the things you see don't change as much as things to either side. You see a far-off tree, then the tree is closer, then it's right there, and then - assuming you didn't drive right into it - it is gone. Your brain has plenty of time to capture and assimilate data, to figure out how stuff is moving relative to you and, based on that information, how important each thing you see is (in terms of your goal, which is often'getting where you are going in one piece'.). You have time to understand what you are seeing, so you feel okay. Things to the side zip by so fast that sometimes we don't have time to even know what we are seeing, and we definitely don't have time to process the visual information with our brains.... by the time our brains have figured out one thing, a few hundred other things have gone last at high speed. This inability to get a mental grasp on what we are looking at (to either side) can make us feel like the ground is slipping out from underneath us, which it is, technically. Vertigo, nausea, motion sickness.... these are all just feelings of un-ease caused by not being able to grasp what we see before it is far behind us. Our brains plus our visual acuity let us know howwhere we stand in relation to everything else. When we are moving, signals from our inner-ear - the seat of balance - help us understand what we are seeing. This can lead to some weird experiences, like when you're stopped at a light and the car next to you starts rolling backwards and you think it's you that is moving.... the information from your eyes and the information from your inner-ear don't match, and you have a moment of panic trying to figure out what is really going on. When you are moving, the road ahead is less likely to contain elements that cause such disparity in our senses.... but looking to the side, that's almost all we see. Focusing on the horizon, which doesn't really change much, instead of focusing on the things zipping by near the vehicle, can reduce or eliminate ill-at-ease feelings like motion sickness. This is such a fundamental process that it even happens when we are not moving, but we are seeing other things move. When filming trains, for instance, the train needs to go faster when it is coming toward the camera or it looks like less of a threat - not much changes from one moment to another - but filming from the side, the train needs to go slower or all we see is motion blur. Filming a train going its normal speed results in images that make us feel something is not right.... adjusting the speed of the train based on the direction it is being filmed helps the image match up with what our eyes, brains, and inner-ear think is happening.

article: A dehumidifier is just an air conditioner that doesn't vent its heat outside. You have a liquid refrigerant that travels through an expansion valve where it's converted into a vapor. The refrigerant then travels through a compressor, which compresses the vapor, causing it to heat up. This hot vapor is then passed through a coil that's cooler than the vapor, causing it to condense back into a liquid. This process releases heat and moisture, which is then collected in a reservoir. The cool liquid refrigerant then travels back to the expansion valve, and the process repeats. The end result is a reduction in humidity in the surrounding air. article: Actually it is because the focus of the two technologies is completely different. Transmission is bit by bit, there may be grouping of bits for error checking reasons, but otherwise each bit has to be sent individually. In contrast memory and storage need to be indexed, by grouping bits of 8 into a byte, you gain significant improvements in performance and reduced cost. So bandwidth is actually sending bits, so focuses on bits, storage is indexed by bytes, so is measured in bytes.','Changing it would be more confusing. Less knowledgeable consumers would be tricked by the fact that all the numbers are 8 times lower now, and more knowledgeable consumers would have to carefully check what units the connection speed was in.','Bits per second is a "natural" unit when talking about how much data can go through a certain connection. It's been a while since I've taken a communications systems course, so forgive me if I'm unclear when explaining this. "Bandwidth" is literally the 'width' of the 'frequency band' at which you are transmitting information. Frequency is measured in cycles per second (or Hz). Each cycle can then transmit only so many symbols without errors, and to compute this you do some math that I can't remember offhand, and that turns cycles-per-second into symbols-per-second. In binary, each symbol is one bit, so engineers naturally talk about transmission rates in bits per second, since that's what they compute when they go from "I have this wire" or "I have this transmitter and receiver" to "I can transmit this much data over it." I hope this made sense. Bits per second is the only reasonable unit for measuring transmission rates, from the perspective of engineers who design things with transmission rates. Bytes are the confusing unit, since computers were designed such that when you get information from them, you get them in chunks of 8 bits (which is then called a byte).', "A network cable doesn't care how you group your data together...all it cares is how many 1's and 0's it can push. Because, surprisingly enough, it doesn't always take 8 bits to sent a byte of information. Data packets have have headers and sometimes parity bits and error correction codes....that's not part of your data, but they still take time to transmit. Some network hardware uses data compression protocols, which mean each byte is likely going to take less than 8 bits to send. You just can't take megabits, divide by 8, and expect that to match your download rates. There is a lot more going on than that.

article: The earpiece is called an IFB (most professionals would say it stands for Interrupted Fold Back... but many fist fights have errupted from this, so different people think it stands for different things) So to answer your question the talent (person with the IFB in the ear) can hear the Fold Back of the show (what you hear at home). The reason it's in the ear and not simply on speakers nearby is the obvious feedback and echo'ing crazyness that would happen. The Interrupt bit means that the producer or director can "interrupt" the audio with instructions. Basically like a PA system at the grocery store... usually you hear music, but when someone presses a button, the music is muted and you hear "cleanup on aisle 3" "What instructions?" you may ask. Well with television timing is everything. Quite frequently "the script" gets changed on the fly. So the producer (who planned and wrote most of the show) will decide what to cut or add and tell the talent what the plan is. The director (who is controlling all the moving parts) also talks to talent, but will usually give very basic instructions like GO or turn to camera 1, or a countdown to break (yes, good talent can hear a 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 countdown in their ear, read the teleprompter AND change the speed of the read to match up with the count) The mic is always on, but not always up in the mix. So the talent can have lengthy conversations during the show with the crew in the control room as long as they're not doing anything on air at the time. There's also something called mix minus... but that gets a little more complicated. Basically, reporters in the field don't want to hear their own mic (because of delays and echos). So the audio engineer will create a special mix just for them; which is the full audio you hear at home MINUS their own mic. It's VERY annoying to hear your own voice coming into your ear two seconda late as you're talking. TL;DR: They hear the show. They also get instructions about the future plans from the producer and countscues from the director. They can't rely on speakers because the audio would cause a feedback loop with the microphone.','Yes you are right with the producer. They are used to alert the anchor of any breaking developments, guide them if they are becoming lost, or insert any additional notes. It is a tricky position because you do not want to talk too much into the anchors ear because they can become confused.','They're also telling them information about the show as it's going on, the sort of nuts and bolts, administrative stuff. article: Depends on the windows version, driver version and USB controller firmware. Even if you don't actively try to execute a file on the USB drive, the USB stick could be another type of USB device in disguise. Even if it looks like an USB drive, it could secretly be pretending to be a USB keyboard as well, and send keyboard commands to your machine, and windows would think they were from a real keyboard. It could also attack the USB hardware controller in your PC, if it has a known weakness, or windows' drivers for it, to load data into RAM and then executing it, without actually having to go through the normal file-transfer protocols. No files would be transferred, but for example the area of your RAM that used to hold your Chrome browser now suddenly contains malicious code from your USB device, and the next time your PC tries to access the chrome browser, the machine would accidentally execute the new code that was put there instead. I don't know why you included the size of the USB stick. That makes no difference. Bottom line, you should not insert USB devices you don't know where came from, unless you have a locked down, isolated computer that you don't mind having to wipe and reinstall. Even if you think your system is patched and up to date, there's still a chance that you might encounter malicious software that attacks a weakness that no one (other than those who made the malware) knows of yet. In fact, dropping infected usb devices on purpose in hope that someone will pick them up and check what's on them has been used to get unauthorized access to systems in the past, and I wouldn't be surprised if it's still used today as well.,Yes. Many USB connected devices provide the driver information necessary for the computer to correctly interact with it. This is how the myriad USB devices can work without having to install separate driver software for each. Malicious software can introduce itself as part of this driver interrogation and negotiation. Sometimes this will be done under the appearance of providing device information, such as "how bug is the storage on this device" or "what is the resolution of this camera" or whatever. Done "right" this device driver interaction will run software on the USB device regardless of you autorun settings. You need to disable automatically enabling USB devices when they are inserted. The computer should then detect some very basic "device present" information. However, to use the device, it still needs to do the aforementioned negotiation. There are USB scanners available that can try to detect malware or undesirable interactions, but they fall under the normal arms race that all malware detection have; if the malware is more sophisticated than the detection, it will likely escape detection. Make sure you have solid antivirus and rootkit detection software and you'll be as protected as you can. Trust no one, and assume the worst habits by those you share USB storage with.

article: The word "frictionless" is a bit awkward here, because if the question is after what I think it's after then friction is important. If you roll something down a ramp it isn't simply falling. Instead, some of the energy is used to make the object spin. That won't happen if the ramp is frictionless, it'll just skid down it. However, if there is friction which allows the ramp to grip the object, (but not perhaps to resist its movement, which I suspect it was it means), then the object with the lowest rotational inertia will arrive first. Again there's a bit of a snag here, because if there's enough friction to spin a wheel, it's probably enough to stop a cube sliding. Never mind, let's assume it's a magic ramp. The cube would arrive first, because none of its potential energy is used to spin it, so all can be converted into kinetic energy. The hoop next, as its rotational intertia is low, then the disc, then the sphere. This is all rather vague, because it's not stated whether they have the same diameter, density, density distribution etc. BUT, as others have said, it it really is without ANY friction (including atmospheric drag) then they'll all arrive at the same time.','I believe your question comes with the implied "in a vacuum" as that's more or less what a friction-less ramp would require. As such they would all hit the ground at the same time.', "If the ramp is indeed frictionless, all four objects would hit the ground at exactly the same time. The weight of an object is equal to it's mass multiplied by the local gravitational field strength (9.81ms2). There is a reaction force from the ramp which is equal to the component of the weight perpendicular to the ramp (this stops the object from passing through the ramp), so the total force on the object is equal to the weight projected in the plane parallel to the ramp, which is the weight multiplied by the sin of the angle the ramp makes with the ground. (In the abscence of any other forces like friction or air resistance). The acceleration of the object is the force divided by the mass, and since the force is proportional to mass, the mass cancels and is irrelevant. The acceleration of each object down the slope depends only on the gravitational field strength and the angle of the slope. The shape of the object doesn't factor in at all if it is assumed that all the objects have settled into a stable configuration (i.e not balanced on a corner).

article: It's about a 10 difference, with the troy ounce (31.1 grams) being heavier than the avoirdupois ounce (standard ounce, 28.35 grams). However, a troy pound (12 troy ounces) is lighter than a standard pound (16 ounces). There was this market place in France, in the city of Troyes, where people came from all around the world to trade. The word probably derives from that market, where they developed a system of measurement that could be used so that all the goods in the market place was the same. That way, no one could be cheated based on the weight of their goods being calculated differently. The system was probably derived from an older system developed by the Romans, where the "pound" was called "aes grave," and the "ounce" was "uncia," defined as 112th of an aes grave. Hence the troy pound being comprised of 12 troy ounces instead of the usual 16 ounces. The avoirdupois ounce is the full name for the standard ounce that we use in everyday measurements. All the stuff at your local grocery store is measured in avoirdupois ounces, your bathroom scale is set that way, the entire Imperial system of measurement uses it. You've probably never heard the full name because we generally just call it "ounces.,'The Troy ounce is a traditional unit of gold weight. (31.1 g) The ounce is used for everything else. (28.35 g)
